criterion_notes.c1: Examines four community-based water supply (CBWS) systems serving 488 households in Salatiga City, Indonesia, framed around sustaining community drinking-water services where the municipal utility (PDAM) does not reach.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper touches on institutional and governance factors because 'Institutional' (comprising Legality of management, Cooperation, SOP, Job Description and Planning, Working Schedule, Internal and External Reporting, Services to customer, and Satisfaction of customers) is evaluated as one of five Rapfish sustainability dimensions and internal committee management practices are discussed. However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is NOT met (c2 = no): the study tests whether physical water source type (deep well vs. spring) influences CBWS sustainability and evaluates generic internal committee management/operational functioning (whether multiple officers vs. only the head are active, presence of SOPs, and internal bookkeeping), rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules governing access, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure). Moreover, even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the full-text decision (plain_criterion2_decision) remains 'exclude' because institutional attributes are treated as an output sustainability dimension rather than an exposure governing access and no disaggregate service-access outcome is reported (fails C4 and C5).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical study collecting primary data (questionnaire surveys with 168 returned questionnaires across 4 CBWS, interviews, and field observations) and secondary organizational/financial data, analyzed via Rapfish multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) and Monte Carlo sensitivity simulation.
criterion_notes.c4: Although Table 1 lists 'Coverage', 'Customer coverage', 'Continuity', and 'Ability to pay' among 35 attributes fed into the Rapfish appraisal, the paper reports only composite 0-100 MDS sustainability scores for five broad dimensions (Ecological, Technological, Social, Institutional, and Economic) and never reports any empirical household or community outcomes for access, connection, coverage, service availability, reliability, continuity, water quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (4 CBWS schemes serving 488 user houses; 168 survey respondents) and study design (cross-sectional multi-case Rapfish MDS appraisal) are identifiable, but an eligible legal/administrative exposure and a relevant service-access outcome cannot be identified as an exposure-outcome pair: water source type (deep well vs. spring) is the main comparative factor, institutional items form one of five output sustainability scores, and access-related items are submerged unreportably inside composite scores.

evidence_quotes.quote: In Salatiga Indonesia, the water supply company (PDAM) can now only serves about 65.64% of the city’s population [2]. There are about 11.14% of the population which are served by community based water supply (CBWS) [2].
The research method uses primary and secondary data collected from each CBWS studied. Primary data consist of questionair survey, interview, and field observation.

The research is performed to 4 (four) CBWS in two Kelurahan at Salatiga City, each represents a deep well and a spring water sources such as shown in Table 2. It is expected to demonstrate whether the source of water has some influences on the sustainability of a CBWS.

Figure 4 shows the Institutional Dimension. It shows that Tirta Barokah and Tirta Sejahtera are in sustainable status (over 50 score). Meanwhile, Tirta Kamandanu and Tirta Agung are very low (not sustainable status), ecah obtain 30.82 and 38.64.

Overall, Tirta Barokah and Tirta Sejahtera are in sustainable status with MDS score are all over 50 which allow them to develop further. The Tirta Kamandanu and Tirta Agung are still having problem internally (institutional and economic), which cause them to be in the status of not sustainable
The type of source water (deep well or springs) does not have significant (determining factor) guaranteeing sustainable CBWS. Rather, it more dependent to its management practices.

raw_response.exposure: Water source type (deep well vs. spring water source) and generic internal CBWS committee management/operational functioning
raw_response.outcome: Composite Rapfish multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) sustainability status index scores (0-100 scale) across Ecological, Technological, Social, Institutional, and Economic dimensions
raw_response.population_and_sample: 4 community-based water supply (CBWS) systems (Tirta Barokah, Tirta Sejahtera, Tirta Kamandanu, and Tirto Agung) in two Kelurahan (Sidorejo Lor and Kauman Kidul), Salatiga City, Indonesia, serving 488 user households (168, 120, 160, and 40 houses; 168 returned questionnaires)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded at full text under E03 (Wrong exposure), and additionally lacks an eligible access outcome (C4). The study appraises the sustainability status of four community-based water supply (CBWS) schemes in Salatiga, Indonesia, using the Rapfish multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) method across five dimensions (Ecological, Technological, Social, Institutional, and Economic). Its designed comparative factor is physical water source type (deep well vs. spring water) alongside generic internal committee management practices (having active committee staff vs. one-person operation, SOPs, and internal reporting), rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing water service access per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope clarification. Furthermore, even under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because 'Institutional' is modeled only as an aggregated sustainability sub-score and the paper reports only composite 0-100 sustainability scores rather than empirical measures of household or community water access, connection, coverage, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional multi-case sustainability appraisal using Rapfish multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) and Monte Carlo sensitivity analysis
